text:
Typical lifecycle decisions and approvals

Approval depth should be proportional to cost, complexity, security exposure, regulatory obligations, and business criticality. Smaller low-risk changes may use automated or delegated approvals, while enterprise releases usually require formal evidence and separation of duties.

Lifecycle stage | Key decisions | Typical approval or gate | Typical accountable roles
Intake and triage | Is the problem worth solving, strategically aligned, and feasible enough to investigate? | Idea accepted, rejected, deferred, or sent to discovery | Business sponsor, product leadership, portfolio management
Discovery and business case | What outcomes, users, benefits, costs, dependencies, and major risks define the initiative? | Business case and funding approved | Executive sponsor, finance, portfolio board
Classification and governance | How complex, critical, regulated, and security-sensitive is the application? What delivery controls apply? | Risk tier, governance path, and required reviewers confirmed | Enterprise architecture, security, risk, compliance
Scope and requirements | What is included, excluded, prioritized, and measurable? What constitutes acceptance? | Scope baseline, requirements, acceptance criteria, and delivery increment approved | Product owner, sponsor, business stakeholders
Solution design | Which architecture, technologies, integrations, data models, and hosting patterns should be used? | Architecture and technical design approved; exceptions formally accepted | Architecture review board, engineering lead, data owner
Security, privacy, and compliance | Are identity, access, data handling, threat controls, retention, and regulatory requirements adequate? | Security and privacy design approved; residual risks accepted by authorized owners | Security, privacy, legal, compliance, risk owner
Delivery readiness | Is the backlog actionable, team funded, environments available, and delivery approach realistic? | Build authorization or iteration commitment | Product owner, delivery lead, engineering lead
Build and change control | Do changes meet coding, review, traceability, configuration, and dependency standards? | Peer review and automated quality gates passed; significant changes approved | Engineering team, repository owners, change authority
Testing and acceptance | Does the application satisfy functional, integration, performance, accessibility, security, and recovery expectations? | Test exit criteria passed and user acceptance granted; defects accepted or resolved | Quality lead, product owner, business representatives, security
Release readiness | Are deployment, migration, rollback, monitoring, communications, training, and support arrangements ready? | Operational readiness and change or release approval | Release manager, operations, service owner, change advisory authority
Production deployment | Should the release proceed, pause, roll back, or expand after initial rollout? | Go or no-go decision and production access authorization | Business owner, technical owner, release authority
Post-release validation | Is the release healthy and producing expected results? | Release accepted, remediated, or rolled back | Product owner, operations, engineering, business owner
Operations and improvement | Which incidents, risks, technical debt, patches, and enhancements should be prioritized? | Service reviews, risk acceptances, maintenance approvals, and backlog decisions | Service owner, product owner, security, operations
Retirement | Should the application be replaced or decommissioned, and how will data and obligations be handled? | Retirement, migration, archival, access removal, and closure approved | Business owner, data owner, architecture, security, records management
limitations: The organization’s governance model, risk tier, and platform-specific approval mechanisms were not identified, so roles and gates are representative rather than prescriptive.
